utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Morning to all. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, and case manager Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honour. On behalf Zupljanin Defence, Dragan Krgovic and Katarina Danicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the witness comes in, can we inquire, because we're now reorganising the witnesses, whether we will be sitting the week after Easter. We heard - I suppose you have to call it a rumour - that we were not. But we assume that because the week is coming off now, we will sitting after Easter. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No. No, we will not be sitting the week after Easter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Dr. Zepinic. I remind that you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. We changed the order. I will start first with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We were introduced a few days ago in the OTP's office, and we had a chance to speak for about five or ten minutes, but let me introduce myself for the transcript. Officially my name is Dragan Krgovic, I'm a member of the Defence team of Stojan Zupljanin, and I will be asking you some questions about your statement. I will be showing you some documents during the cross-examination, documents that we haven't had the chance seeing. I don't believe that you have seen them recently. So I have compiled a set of documents, some of which are there Serbian only. And on the screen, documents are exhibited page by page, but to facilitate communication when I say to you, document so-and-so, you will be able to see it on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to pass this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do I understand there are some documents without a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They're on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we weren't notified that this was happening. And it really doesn't help, because all we get is, then, such part as is shown on the screen in e-court, which may be only part of the document, and we don't know what the context is. I do think if this is the situation, we ought to be told about this in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could counsel enlighten me as to why this seems to be a recurring problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because we -- four days ago we sent the list and indicated some of these documents still pending or translation. The main problem is the summary of this witness, because we received a summary with two paragraph doesn't mention my client at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I hear you, but I'm not sure that that answers the concern raised by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue in B/C/S. When we received the summary and when we started preparing for this witness and nothing was pointing to any connection between him and my client. It wasn't mentioned in the summary or in the proofing notes what this witness would be testifying about. As a result, the Defence, only after the examination-in-chief and the mention of some documents, indicated that this evidence would also deal with the role of my client. So that all documents that we sent off for translation were not all translated. Some are either on the 65 ter list or were submitted in the latest disclosures in the past month or so. So we didn't have time to translate them all. But what we were able to do, we have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there a practical solution that you propose to the immediate problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I will show the document -- show the witness the documents, and have him read out the letterhead, and then I will only deal with some paragraphs from the documents. These are mostly documents that were sent to this witness by Mr. Zupljanin, and they relate to the events in which this witness was also involved. The witness is familiar with the documents, and the events that I will be mentioning are events in which he took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the reason why we agreed for me to start with the cross-examination is for the OTP to have some time to verify the context of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, is there a response.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not really, Your Honour. I don't quite follow that. Our list of documents that was going to be shown to Mr. Zepinic, Dr. Zepinic, was sent to the Defence, whatever it was, the day before he started testifying. They notified us of the documents they were going to be using as he started testifying, so it cannot be right to say that because of -- it's only because of his examination-in-chief that they have decided to use these documents. My only concern is - I don't want to stop them - is that unless we have these documents in -- in translation, as I said, we can't see the context. Presumably on the list they've indicated which of the ones they haven't got a translation for, and have they sent -- well, I see Mr. Smith says not. And equally I would like the whole document. You see, Your Honours, the e-mail we got says we are still awaiting for translation for most of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all these documents have been in e-court for at least five days. It was indicated that they would be used in this case, and once we received the OTP's list of documents and when the examination-in-chief in started, we submitted this list. It wasn't my intention to cross-examine this witness at all. If the Prosecutor and the examination-in-chief through the documents and through the questions put to this witness hadn't dealt with some issues, I wouldn't be examining Mr. Zepinic at all. But, due to this decision by the OTP and due to the lack of information in the proofing notes and the summary, we have put in this situation. So this wasn't expected. So I only want to go through some documents briefly with the witness. I will read out the -- the headings and have him look at the signatures and the like. And, actually, these are documents that we received from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, among our concerns is that notwithstanding your representation that the Prosecution would have time to look at these documents, how long in fact are they? And this is all in the context of the commitment, undertaking, whatever the proper word is, that this witness is to be released today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has a good memory, so these documents are just a prop for me to remind him of some events and details thereof. The documents are a few pages long, but I don't want to go through all of them, just the heading or the signature or possibly a paragraph or two from each in order to ask the witness whether he remembers the events or the information related to them. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This is the third time you have indicated that. But the practical problem, as Ms. Korner has highlighted, is that once they would have seen the full document, there may be a context which they would wish properly to be able to address. And given the time constraints that we are under today, is -- would the Prosecution be in a position to deal with any possible concerns that they may have, once they would have had the advantage of seeing the entire document to which, admittedly, you say you're only putting the signature and the caption to the witness. That's the practical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can proceed differently. I can ask the witness about some events, whether he knows about them, and then, without using the documents, go on in a different manner. It was only my intention to help the witness remember some things, but 90 per cent of the documents were sent to the witness anyway originally. And these are the documents that were disclosed to us by the OTP, and they are certainly in their possession. These are not our documents. They are all documents received from the OTP. They bear the signature of my client, and the witness was a participant to those events. I believe it is all a simple matter. We shouldn't waste more time on such procedural issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which is exactly the point that I was going to make. I suggest that we begin, and see where we get. And we proceed document by document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, I apologise for this --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for saying that I had a good memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, you are the right person to clarify some things concerning the Special Police and some other police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see on e-court document 2D02-0848. I apologise. The last four figures are 0878.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can find it under tab 1, sir, the very first document. When you spoke about the Special Police and other police detachments, you said that in some CSBs of some municipalities there were such units, units that were called special units, but probably you meant manoeuvre units that could be found in any CSB and the members of which were also in SJBs.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We called them manoeuvre units or special units, and every CSB established them from the personnel of the police stations under the CSBs. They were manned mostly by younger and well-trained police officers, and in the police stations, they were members of the manoeuvre or special units. And our MUP special unit was also a manoeuvre unit. So whichever way you choose to call them, the manoeuvre or special unit in the CSB of Banja Luka, that was a unit that Mr. Zupljanin could deploy with the approval of the ministry. That is us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the document in front of you shows the total strength of the reserve forces, and it includes the manoeuvre unit; is that correct? You can see that it is dated the 21st of December 1989, and it is signed by Slobodan Djuric, head of unit -- head of section, who was in charge of these things at the time.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was Djuric, Slobodan. I can't answer that question. Obviously he was, but, as I said, in any CSB there was a certain unit that dealt with issues concerning the reserve forces, including the manoeuvre or special unit, that would be established according to need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this document speaks about that, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It shows a number of the members of the reserve forces of -- by CSB Banja Luka and the number -- the strength of the manoeuvre special unit that could be activated in case of need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And here in line one where it reads "number of police stations;" then to the right we can read "manoeuvre unit;" and in the extreme right, "total strength."

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, there were 13 police stations in the Banja Luka municipality. They were SJBs or traffic police stations. And out of the total personnel, amounting to 825 in the SJBs in Banja Luka, 170 were members as -- manoeuvre units in the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this manoeuvre unit has nothing to do with the special unit that was in Sarajevo, commanded by Dragan Nikic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it had. Because they were connected through equipment and for training purposes and in case of need. The manoeuvre unit that would be deployed in the area of Banja Luka would act in co-operation with the one from Sarajevo if, according to our estimate, the local manoeuvre unit were unable to deal with the situation, then we would also deploy our own manoeuvre unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But I thought with regard to the establishment of units that they were different.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. But in case of need, the special unit of the MUP could intervene in the Banja Luka area and, according to need, use part or all of the manoeuvre structures that were present in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to mark this document for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Krgovic, who issued the documents and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was issued by the SUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo. And it is signed by Slobodan Djuric, head of section. And it speaks about the very issue I -- that Mr. Zupljanin is concerned with, namely, the manning or the composition of the manoeuvre units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, this document appears to be issued on the 21st of February, 1989, which was well in advance of the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exactly, in advance of the appointment of the witness. So my question would be does this also reflect the situation after April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understood the witness, and that's why I asked him because he was in the MUP, about the -- how the manoeuvre unit was established and how the system functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, can you confirm that at the time while you were at MUP the principle reflected in this document was respected?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, once we came to power we didn't changed the strength of the manoeuvre units or the reserve forces, but in agreement with the chiefs of police stations in the field, we launched some operational activities concerning staff, which -- to the effect that manoeuvre units be better equipped with staff. But we didn't change the strength of the -- the manoeuvre unit or the active police forces, or, indeed, the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't change the organisational structure either. It was the same as shown in this document. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D37, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, I'm sure that you're aware of the fact that in 1991 war broke out Croatia, and that as a result of war operations, the situation, the security situation changed dramatically in the territory covered by the CSB Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As a result of that, the MUP, which is your institution, and other relevant political and state organs, started receiving reports about the situation becoming more aggravated in the border area with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As a result, you felt a need to strengthen the police force and to undertake certain measures. There were requests from CSB to deal with the issue.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the personnel issues. In other terms, we were not able to deal with the problems that spilled over from Croatia, once the war broke out in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The MUP, on its own, and when I say the MUP, I mean the Ministry of Interior in Sarajevo, was not able to deal with the issues itself, because the circumstances were not depending on the MUP.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not within our purview to deal with the security and other political issues that could be felt in the regions of Banja Luka, Bihac, Western Herzegovina, Slovenia and Semberija at the moment when war broke out in Croatia. So not only MUP, but other bodies of power were involved in all that, including the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document 2D02085 -- 85.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, Mr. Zepinic, the document is under tab 2. This document was issued by the CSB. It is a letter which was sent on the 27th of August, 1991, and we see the list of addressees. Let's start with the bottom address, the Deputy Minister, that was you; the minister; to the executive council of the SRBH Assembly; to the SRBH Assembly; to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and to Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You forgot the deputy prime minister, Mr. Simovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had forgotten him. Could you please turn to page 2 of this document. And will you see that the signatory of the document is Stojan Zupljanin. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask you whether you remember having received this document.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you whether I received the document or not. But given the fact that it was addressed to me, I'm sure that I received it. And if you have questions about the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the answers provided by Mr. Zupljanin in his letter, on several occasions at the meetings of the government and the Presidency, we requested the enlargement of the personnel of the active strength of the police, as well as additional materiel and technical equipment for public security stations. Unfortunately, we did not receive the green light either from the Presidency or the government for various reasons which are beyond the scope of interest of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with the issues, and you are familiar with the context of this letter?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with all that. It was very present in all CSBs, not only in Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in this letter, in its first paragraph, due to the critical and dramatic war circumstances around the border - and this is something I already asked you about - Stojan Zupljanin requests some things.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the minister we agree with that, and as you can see Mr. Zupljanin says in the letter that the personnel had undergone the required medical checkups in the centre for health protection in our ministry. So as far as the ministry was concerned, there was no problem. The only problem was who was going to pay for all that. Let's not embark on political issues and talk about the required number of police officers. It says here that Mr. Zepinic [as interpreted] requested the increase in the strength of the police force, and this bothered everybody else because everybody thought that if we increased the number of our personnel we would do something else and not what we put forth as the reason for the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this document please be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I'm sorry to say, this is altogether completely blurred to me. You have the benefit of being able to understand what the letter says, but I not. And according to the witness's testimony, it's -- it's completely obscure to me what this letter is about and what the numbers are that are referred to in the documents. So I don't know if could you be more helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'll try and be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, in this document I have provided its summary, but it wasn't enough. Mr. Zupljanin requests an increase in the number of personnel in the centres due to the war circumstances in Croatia. And on the last page he refers to the number of personnel that had to be employed. He says that they had undergone medical checkups, that the ministry had approved all that, but those men still hadn't been appointed, and he requests assistance. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before you decide whether to mark it for identification or not, could I have a query. Mr. Krgovic said these documents came from us. This one doesn't have an ERN anywhere to be seen, so I'd like to know where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is from the batch of exculpating material, number 68. I don't know whether I received it from the government of Republika Srpska, from the centre for cooperation The Hague Tribunal. I'm sure that I saw some of the documents in question. Just a moment. I'm going check in any case. Because I have a set of documents that I received from the centre for cooperation. I believe I have it, and I will double-check during the break, and I will inform the Prosecutor about the provenance. But for the time being, can this document please be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose for practical purposes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D38, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, you certainly received quite a number of similar reports which described the situation, the problems, the war in the territory which was within the authority of the CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Those reports spoke about explosions, paramilitary units, and the incidents in the territory of the centre. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You certainly received regular reports which were submitted either quarterly, annually, or every six months, as needed.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every CSB was duty-bound to regularly submit their reports on work and the security situation in the territory. And they also had a duty, and it was common practice of every police station and CSB to also assess the situation regularly and send dispatches to the ministry about any incidents as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As a result of the need that arose, you, in agreement with other relevant factors, in order to calm the situation down and to check what happened, at one point you went to visit the territory of the centre as a member of a commission.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you that I went only once. I travelled frequently and visited several areas, either on my own, with my associates, with other government members. And every time I went to an area, I spoke to the relevant personnel in order to try and resolve the situation. As soon as I received reports from the field, the ministry informed the government and the presidents about the deterioration of the security situation and requested further instructions and assistance from the other bodies who might have been of assistance in dealing with any conflict situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 2D04004.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which, Mr. Zepinic, is number 7 in your binder. Mr. Zepinic, this is a document issued by the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which speaks about various visits to municipalities of Banja Luka, Bosanska Gradiska, Bosanski Dubica, and Bosanski Novi and information about the security situation in those municipalities. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, you can see that -- let's wait for the document to appear on e-court before I put my question to you. Nikola Koljevic, a member of the Presidency, visited the municipalities in question, and on behalf of Ministry of the Interior, under paragraph 2, you will see that Vitomir Zepinic, the Deputy Minister of the interior; Avdo Hebib, the Assistant Minister were members of that delegation and that there was also Miro Radovic and Djordje Jancevski. You see this in the document, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Miro Radovic was the assistant chief of state security, and Djordje Jancevski was the chief of administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they were there.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with Dr. Koljevic on behalf of the Presidency we toured the ground in order to verify the situation in the territory of the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And further on it says that there were talks with the leadership of Banja Luka municipality with the participation of the Banja Luka corps, the chief of security of Banja Luka, and the chief of security stationed in Banja Luka, and that you also visited refugees in various settlements?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we visited a group of refugees who were accommodated, as far as -- if memory serves me properly, in two schools. They had fled Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please make pauses between questions and answers and try not to overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The interpreters, once again, are asking you to pause between questions and answers, both for you and the witness. So please observe a small pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zepinic, further on reference is made to the topics discussed at the meeting. And the first one is the security situation in the municipalities of Bosanski Dubica, Bosanska Gradiska, and Bosanski Novi. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Further on in page 2 in the third paragraph from the bottom it says that unique assessment on the part of all the participants in the talks was that the situation in the municipalities bordering on the Republic of Croatia from Derventa to Bosanska Kostajnica had all the characteristics of aggravating circumstances. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I agree because we had a war on our door-step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Further on, there's certain observations made by the bodies of the interior. And in the next paragraph, or the three following paragraphs, 5, 6, and 7, a reference is made to the increased presence of members of the MUP Croatia in the areas bordering on Bosnia, that there are -- the control measures were stepped up. And finally in the last paragraph reference is made to the entrance of MUP specials from Croatia into Bosanski Novi, as well as the appearance of individuals and smaller groups of members of MUP Croatia in the territory of the SRBH in uniform. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such occasions. You have to bear in mind that members of the MUP of Croatia, or a lot of them from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did arrive and attended several meetings with Mr. Gojko Susak [as interpreted] who was the minister of the interior of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Mr. Boljkovac.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I pointed to the problems that those men who arrived for visits arrived uniforms with no arms and that that caused additional security problems in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that that represented a problem that the Ministry of Croatia should bear in mind, because any presence of men in uniform from Croatia or from any other state for that matter was an additional cause of the aggravation of the security situation and the increase of tensions in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will not go through the rest of the document which speaks about a series of incidents in that area. Please go on to page 4 of this document, where it says that: "With regard to the overall situation in the area of the CSB, the local forces cannot cope with the current conditions with regard to the manpower at their disposal or their equipment." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully. And that's why we requested from the cabinet and the Presidency to approve strengthening the MUP and approve additional equipment. But they -- we never received that approval. I don't want to go into the reasons for that. But we tried, through cooperation with the MUPs of Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro, and the federal MUP, which still was in existence at the time, as well as the General Staff, to integrate the overall security system to prevent the escalation of the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question about this document, on page 5, we can read that it was observed that the CSB of Banja Luka and the SJBs of Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Gradiska, and Bosanski Dubica, as far as their personnel strength and materiel equipment allows, did all within their power to stop the negative trends, but the efficiency was limited due to their modest number -- strength of personnel and modest technical abilities, which was partly made up for by mutual assistance. Can -- as you confirmed, is that true?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was present at the Presidency session when this was discussed, and they -- where they said that -- criticism was uttered of the cabinet of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because they failed to respond to the situation in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I seem to have read too fast for the interpreters. So I read out that the deployment of the organs of the republic, except for the MUP, hardly -- hardly took place at all. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to mark this document for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, first of all, I missed the date of this document. Secondly, I fail to see the relevance of this -- this document as you have explained, or as the witness has explained, seems to though that the security situation in Banja Luka, among other places, was being destabilized as a consequence of the imminent threats of war in Croatia and so that the chiefs of the CSBs in the regions affected by this were asking for reinforcements, and they didn't get it. This is the second document that you are showing to the witness this morning which seems to -- to -- tentative to document this. But what exactly is the point that you wish the Court to draw from this? I mean, after all, it is not surprising that when a war is building up, then inevitably the security situations in the surrounding areas is also affected. So if this is all that you want to show, then I fail to see the relevance. But I may have missed the point, and so please be helpful to the Court and try explain what it is that you want to show with this document. And finally, thirdly, the document seems to be not immediately overseeable in the sense that it is a document that goes on for five or six pages or even more, I don't know. So the context may be difficult for the Chamber and, indeed, for the Prosecution to understand also. Can you clarify on these three points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to draw an analogy through this witness, namely that the situation in the Banja Luka region at the time when the witness was Deputy Minister of the interior was disastrous with interethnic conflict that later escalated into war. And that explosions, arson, et cetera, were a consequence of those events, rather than a planned and systematic action incited by the SDS, as the OTP alleged, or by other organs that were controlled by the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Likewise, that, in that context, concrete action was taken which I will show based on the following document. A joint action was launched by this witness and my client to the effect that up until 1992 all ethnic groups are treated equally and that the problems in the MUP and in the CSB were not that serious. And these are the events in which this witness participated, together with my client, in trying to prevent that from happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krgovic, how does this speak to your case? What -- what significance does this have to the defence of your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is relevant, like the Prosecutor says, to know the wider context of the behaviour of the defendant in that period and his participation in the joint criminal enterprise from late 1991 to 1992. That is the period about which this witness is about to speak some more. And the concrete actions that we will get to, I would -- I wanted to show what the real situation was and which activities were taken, arrests, and the behaviour of the centre in the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How long is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document has six pages, but this is the last or maybe the last-but-one that is not translated. And I will no longer use untranslated documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D39, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, as a result of all these events in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in the Banja Luka region, paramilitary formations arrived and armed groups that had come from Croatia and became a serious security problem.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, went to the combat theatre in -- in Croatia and then returned. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the CSB or Mr. Zupljanin reported to you about that in detail, and you were acquainted with the problems in the region. Right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I would have liked him to give me more details about the security situation in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, as a result of the problems with the paramilitary formation, you went to Banja Luka, and together with Stojan Zupljanin and some others, took some steps to arrest that paramilitary formation and have them tried; correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: These were Croatian paramilitaries; is that correct? And what were they prosecuted for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, these were Serb paramilitary formations. I'm about to show a document now. Could we see document 2D0645 on e-court. I apologise, the number is 695. This document is translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] There is no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have it. [Interpretation] The English translation is marked 2D02-0943 for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I ask that if -- this has obviously been uploaded later because we didn't get a copy when he printed these out, but if translations are uploaded later we can be notified so that we can actually print them out ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to place this on the ELMO. This is the English translation for the sake of the Chamber and the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, Your Honours, it is in e-court, but it wasn't in e-court when we were given the original list. So presumably it is a late translation. So I'm asking that we be notified if you upload something in e-court later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation was received very recently. But if we have it in e-court, then we don't need it on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, this document can be found under tab 8 in your binder. It's meant to inform you, and it's addressed to you, about the conduct of armed groups in the area of the CSB. Do you remember receiving this document?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember this particular document. But I remember receiving various documents and reports that came in about the worsening of the security situation in the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To what end, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender it because we have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No. I mean, apart from it being addressed to the witness, what's -- what's the connection -- how is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it speaks about the behaviour of paramilitary formations in the region covered by the CSB of Banja Luka, and the witness knows the context -- context of this document and its content, that's what I asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do we have the report which is allegedly enclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, that is the following document. So could we now show Exhibit 2D030381 to the witness. And this document is translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can you find it under tab 10 in your binder, sir. This is a report on the criminal and other unlawful activities of Veljko Milinkovic and other members of paramilitary formations from the area of Prnjavor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It is dated December 2nd, 1991, and please look at the last page. It is signed by Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but it cannot be the report which is enclosed with the last letter, which is dated September. I appreciate this report I know about. I'm just asking about the September report which is allegedly enclosed with the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I received this from the Prosecutor in the sequence I'm showing them now. So one document follows another. I didn't change the order of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, the document, the first document that was shown to Dr. Zepinic was a letter of the 30th of September, enclosing a report, apparently, or whatever the date it was. So it -- 23rd of September. Which is not one of our documents, because it has no ERN number. The document that is now being shown, this report in December is certainly a document from us, but it is not -- it cannot be the document enclosed with the letter dated the 23rd of September. That's my query. So that's what I asked. Where is the report that goes with that letter? Which, the letter does not come from our collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Krgovic, I thought the report that you were about to put up would have been the other part of the -- what you were seeking to exhibit, in other words, the letter and its accompanying document. But clearly this cannot be the report, as Ms. Korner has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, my mistake. The problem is that I do have the report dated September 30th, but it is not translated. But its content is similar to the content of this one, so -- but can I show the report dated September 30th. I apologise once more for making this mistake. I wanted to avoid using untranslated documents and instead focused on translated documents in order to speed up things. Could we please see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, with respect, it is insufficient to say that the other -- the untranslated document is in substance the same as the one that is now up. Could we -- having regard to the fact that you now appreciate that that wasn't translated, if you wish to deal with the present document, the December document, then, phrase your question accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is more than that. These are not documents that we have. It is one of the concerns that I have, that documents are being produced which we have never seen, and the OTP cleared out the CSB in Banja Luka in 1998. My concern is, firstly, the provenance of these document; secondly, that if a letter is put in saying, Here's a report, we get the report that that goes with it. That has not been uploaded into e-court. So, therefore, I object to the production of the -- and certainly MFI'g the letter of the, whatever it was, 30th of September, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber had not ruled on that application.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But I want to make it clear that part documents like this, if is a document is to be put in, the full document must go in. Otherwise, it is misleading in the extreme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Didn't the forwarding letter of 23 September 1991 have the ERN number 2D02/0943?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Never mind.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, your microphone is on. Could you please switch it off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Our numbers have a particular stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a storm in a teacup. Much ado about nothing. These documents were downloaded quite a long time ago, we received from the Republika Srpska or rather from the centre for cooperation with the Tribunal. I will do an additional checkup to make sure that all -- the Prosecutor already has all the documents and that all of them are ERN numbers or at least the Prosecution number. We requested all these documents from the commission for cooperation with the Tribunal in Banja Luka, based on the Prosecutor's documents. Until this is resolved, I'm going to ask for all the documents to be marked for identification, and then I will submit the relevant number of the documents to the Prosecutor. However, at the end of the day, I just wanted to make things easier for the witness. I can put questions to him even without documents, but I will have an objection from the Prosecutor, like with the last witness. That's why I decided to use documents, and that was the whole essence of me using the documents in the first place, or opting for the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection -- can I make this absolutely clear, I have no objection to the documents being used hopefully with translations, provided the full document is given to us. That's all, at the moment, my objection relates to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, whatever we had we submitted to the Prosecutor, and that is the point. And the only problem is the fact that the translations are missing, as far as can I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm sorry to waste time like this. But Mr. Krgovic has just waived the report which he says was attached to the letter, but we haven't got it because it has not been uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just check the number of this 30 September report. Just a moment. Please bear with me. 2D030381. I apologise, Your Honours, 2D020705 is the correct number of the document. Your Honours, this is the 30 September report. I'm not going to be using it with the witness, because I have just decided to avoid using any documents in the further course of cross-examination just to avoid wasting the Trial Chamber's time and provoking the Prosecutor to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good. So we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, because of the problem with translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the record and for the sake of clarity, the -- not-yet-ruled-upon application to mark for identification the September letter, we rule that it should not be so marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, let's speed things along. I'm sure that you know that when you arrived that certain measures were taken and that that group headed by Veljko Milinkovic and members of the Serb paramilitary formations were apprehended, disarmed, and then, in cooperation with the military and investigative organs, they were brought in and incarcerated. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That was an operation under your command or coordinated by you, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Together with Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. [In English] Can I say something more about this particular event because it is quite interesting to explain. It was decision by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina to take action against paramilitary formations and the paramilicia that we had in Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Serb military formations that had arrived from where exactly, and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Those were Serb military para formations from Bosnia and Herzegovina, a group headed by Mr. Milinkovic. If my memory serves me well there were some 60 of them who crossed the border of Croatia and participated in war there, and then returned to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their presence was detrimental for the security situation in Banja Luka. Mr. Zupljanin and his associates informed us regularly about all that, and I, in turn, informed about that the government and the Presidency. The Presidency appointed Mr. Simovic as the vice-president of the government for internal affairs and myself were appointed to hold a meeting with General Uzelac which took place at his command. Mr. Simovic was not present, and I asked from General Uzelac, given my view that the police in Banja Luka was unable to arrest that group, that was well armed and had a lot of experience from the -- previous theatres of war, I requested them to give me his consent for the military police to give us support in arresting Milinkovic and his group. This was, indeed, done. And that was done by the manoeuvre unit of the Banja Luka security services centre with my full consent and with my coordination, and so Mr. Milinkovic and his group - and can you see it in the document - on 15th of November, was remanded in custody in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, if I understand you correctly, we are speaking of a group of Bosnian Serb paramilitaries who came from somewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina in November 1991, crossed the boarder from Bosnia into Croatia and took part in the armed conflict there on the Serb side, I suppose, against the Croatians. And then returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina and billeted themselves in Banja Luka where they created problems. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we did not understand each other. [In English] We are talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This is exactly why it is important to be clear about these matters. Otherwise, the Chamber will have no use -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are talking -- yes, all right. Your Honour, we are talking about paramilitary Serbs -- Serbs from Bosnia being involved in war in Croatia, coming back from Croatia into Bosnia, because they, you know, citizens of Bosnia. They live there. Fully equipped with military equipment, you know, weapons or something like that. Making security and other, I would say, functioning including -- [Interpretation] And let me just note that, Mr. Milinkovic forced the president of the municipality in Prnjavor to leave his office, to take his clothes off and remain only in his shorts, and leave the office. I apologise to the ladies. That was the kind of criminal behaviour that my service could not tolerate irrespective of any support that they may have received from anybody, either from Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's why I asked the government and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to allow me to activate the manoeuvre unit in Banja Luka, in order to arrest that criminal group, and that was, indeed, done. The operation was headed by Mr. Zupljanin, coordinated by myself. We carried out professional part or our involvement, and that action was carried out in a fully professional manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. And this was, indeed, my understanding of your testimony a while ago. But what exactly did this group do, other than forcing gentleman to strip his clothes in his office? How did they pose a threat to the security in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that group was well armed. They had returned from Croatia. That group ill-treated all the citizens. That group disarmed police members at certain check-points. That group threatened the population with arms and in all sorts of other ways. During the investigation we obtained information that they had also been involved in financial crimes and the resale of arms stolen in Croatia, in Kosovo, and then also the resale of stolen fuel that was then sold in the territory of Banja Luka. So the only -- it was not just that they had weapons and threatened the population and they decided to shoot those weapons at any occasion, but that group was also involved in other criminal activities in the general territory of the former Yugoslavia, and not only in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the territory of the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zepinic, it sounds to me as if this group of paramilitaries were terrorising the population in Banja Luka in general. So it wasn't only directed against Croatians or Muslims; it was just a general nuisance to everyone that lived in Banja Luka area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krgovic, if this is correctly understood, then how is this relevant to the defence of your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you look at the documents, you will see that they were a general security threat. However, most of their activities and actions were targeted Muslim and Croatian populations. That's why I wanted to show the Trial Chamber a report dated 5 December 1991 which speaks about the individual cases, such as the case of physical or bodily harm inflicted on Cemal Najib [as interpreted] who was a Muslim, and that total number of such incidents given the fact that they were an ethnically uniform formation, composed of only one ethnicity, and the fact that they were active, how did that influence interethnic relationship and fear among the Muslims. And all that is contained in this report that I was going to show to the witness and as my next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't object to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My I assist? It may not be clear at the moment, but the Milinkovic and the Wolves of Vujic figure quite strongly in the events that tool place in the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That may well be, Ms. Korner, but my problem is that this contradicts what the witness has just told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, that's a matter for the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, it is passed time for the break. We have to continue to consider this. We return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two matters before the usher enters the witness inside the courtroom. First, I would like the record to show that 1D91, which was MFI'd document, it was MFI'd due to requested revision of translation. The revision has been received, and it has been uploaded in the e-court. And, therefore, I would move the Trial Chamber to admit the 1D91, as -- as exhibit. That's one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: 1D91 according to my notes was a letter from Stanisic dated 17th July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To all CSB requesting information on security and crimes, et cetera, on a daily basis. We MFI'd it, according to my notes, for the verification of the date. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That -- that is correct, Your Honour. There was a verification of translation, because the translation was not corresponding to the original document. And now this -- this document with the revised translation has been received and uploaded in e-court, and, therefore, I'm asking the Trial Chamber now to admit the document fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we lift the MFI qualification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the second matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the second matter is, Your Honours, we requested four hours of cross for this witness. Now, I'm mindful of the -- of the Trial Chamber's decision to -- to have the extended sitting for one session in the afternoon. Therefore, I don't know how long Mr. Krgovic will have of his cross-examination, but I just want to -- I just want to inform the Trial Chamber that we are -- that we are very close to four hours right now overall -- of overall time for the cross-examination. At this point already. Thank you very much. What I was trying to say -- we don't -- we don't know at this point whether we will use the whole four hours, but maybe it would be -- it would make sense that we notify the translation department, or whoever we need to notify, that there might be additional time that is required in the afternoon, if possible, of course. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, could you assist us by indicating how much time you think you have left in cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have five or six questions and two documents, that's all. Let's say 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, are you asking for more than one additional session this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we are not asking for anything that we haven't asked before. We asked for four hours of cross. Now if we add to the remaining -- the remaining hours plus one session, I believe we are almost we are at four hours at this point, or even a bit less than four hours. So what we are asking is that we are given the full four hours. If that means that we need to have an additional part of the second session in the afternoon, so ... there might be a need for that. We don't know at this point, Your Honours. I just wanted to put the Trial Chamber on notice about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- before the Chamber decides on this, we need to know what the position of the accused persons are, because the immediate an obvious personal disadvantage to them is that a -- a further extended session impinges on their exercise time and those ancillary considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. Maybe we can continue, and in the meantime find out if that is -- what the position of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, the problem is the arrangements with the Registry has to make -- has to be notified as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you give us a moment, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We can communicate with our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is no problem with the accused, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, let us continue. I will try not to dwell on documents too much. Let us see document 2D030381 in e-court, please. And, Mr. Zepinic, you can find it at tab 10. This is a report about the criminal activities of Veljko Milinkovic, who later led the paramilitary formation, the Wolves from Vucjak, and he is mentioned as the perpetrator of many crimes against the Muslim and Croatian populations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the last part of his question. It was too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, unfortunately, the interpreters did not catch the last part of your question so they ask that you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Essentially what I wanted to ask has been interpreted so that it is okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: But the witness's reply was not translated. So could the witness please repeat also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, could you be good enough to repeat your answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked whether I was familiar with his criminal activity after his arrest, and my reply was negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, on page 4 of this document, where there is a description of the misdeeds of this group, it says that Milan Hajrudinic [phoen], a member shot five shots from his fire-arm and wounded a person whose name we didn't catch. It's on page 4. A Muslim, obviously. It was obviously a crime against a Muslim. And the second part, so the second paragraph where it says that the illegal activity of this group in the area of Prnjavor, which had been going on for months causing fear and discomfort, created a rather electrified situation among the staff of the police due to numerous provocations and direct attacks on the -- on the police staff. This activity also further aggravated inter-ethnic tensions because this group consisted only of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the ethnic composition of Milinkovic's group, nor did I care. I was interested in what the security services could do to stop the -- this illegal activity, this intimidation of the population, including Muslims. That is, intimidation of the population looting and threatening persons with fire-arms. I wanted this group to be eliminated. But I cannot speak about the ethnic composition of that group, nor was I at all interested in it. I was interested in taking all measures possible to eliminate that group, and make it impossible for to them to continue, especially since they had been as brazen to attack a police station and members of the SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Only one part is missing, when you spoke that you were not interested in the ethnic composition and of the attacks on Muslims, although Mr. Zupljanin had informed you that entered.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that they intimidated some Muslims in the area, they threatened them, and they even looted their houses. But they did the same to persons of other ethnicities in the Banja Luka area, so that they were a general -- generally dangerous for the population and the security services in the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now you -- you omitted to say the part that I want to hear, of which you were informed that Mr. Zupljanin --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that his deputy, Bajazid, if I remember well, a Muslim, also informed me in one of his phone calls that the Muslim population in the Banja Luka region was extremely discomforted due to these threats. Also due to the fact the members of these groups were exclusively Serbs, but that wasn't anything that I cared about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And on page 7, if you turn to that page, it says that the investigative magistrate, the last sentence in this paragraph of the court in Prnjavor, ruled on detention and that concluded your part of -- that put an end to your role in this.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, you also received information that, among the refugees, either Serbs or Croats that pass the through the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a certain number of members of armed forces was hiding. I will show you a document dated the 5th of December, and that will be my last document. It is Exhibit 2D020682. This document essentially speaks about an incident at Kljuc, where, on the occasion of the passing through of a convoy of refugees, a number of ZNG members was detected; that is, Croatian soldiers who didn't have any ID on them. Please look at the document, page 2, the third paragraph from the top, where there's a -- a general description, and it goes on on page 3.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me where exactly the document is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can find it at tab 15. I apologise; I didn't mention that. Basically on this second page, it says when a convoy passes a state border and has a security escort, the -- normally the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina had to be informed, and they would be escorted by police. That was usual practice, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It obviously follows from this report that this wasn't the case here, and we can read that in the last paragraph, that this convoy was checked, and a certain number of persons wearing MUP uniforms were found.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this particular incident, but I know that we had a problem with some convoys which were sometimes escorted by the European community monitors or the Red Cross. But among those persons there were sometimes people without any personal documents or persons that had taken part in the combat in Croatia on either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the regular police procedure would have been when this convoy was being checked for those people to produce their IDs, and if they hadn't any, they would have been detained to verify their identity.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But most of the refugees that arrived were without any personal documents so that was an additional problem for the operational services in the area where such convoys were stopped, in order to check the identity of these persons. It was impossible to do so, where they were from, so frankly, we didn't know what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And normally since they were all conscripts, the police and military organs were also included to conduct the necessary checkups.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we included all relevant factors in Bosnia-Herzegovina to establish the identity of these persons to the -- to the extent possible, because this was -- this occurred very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And since these people came mostly by way of Kljuc or Mrkonjic Grad that was mostly the route of those convoys, if you know that.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer as to the routes of those convoys and where they were coming from. I remember that there were huge problems with the establishment of the identity of persons on these convoys and who wore various uniforms. Whether they were members of armed forces in their country, Croatia, we were unable to tell, but there were persons in uniform among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with regard to the witness's reply, I would like to mark this document for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D40, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, finally, you mentioned that you knew Mr. Zupljanin and that you had contacts with him while you were an executive in the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I'm referring to the period in which you collaborated. And as far as can I tell from your evidence, he was a fair co-worker of yours?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything to the contrary. He carried out instructions passed on to him from the MUP. I can -- I know now that there was some dispatches that he sent out behind my back, but, well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Probably it was about a problem that cannot be taken care of in the framework of the MUP, and you saw that some documents I showed you were not only addressed to you only, but almost all relevant in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So if you want to resolve a problem that doesn't depend on the MUP only, so you tried to find support wherever you can find it, right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did require my co-workers from the field to send copies of any reports that say are sent to me to persons that covered security issues from the cabinet or the assembly. It was a sort of attempt to show, if nothing else, that other institutions and persons should be worrying about the security situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina too, and not only me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the burden of dealing with some problems that reflect on the work of the MUP was handed over to a higher level.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political parties should have dealt with some issues through their agreement, but that hot potato was often transferred to the Ministry of the Interior. Instead of dealing with the political issues in the political way, things were done differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just for the moment, going back to the transcript at line 18: "Q. Probably it was about the problem it cannot be taken care of in the," it then reads, "FYROM work." Which is, by my understanding, the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. I don't know what the question was, but it can't have been that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It has been recorded wrongly. I asked you about the problem in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that could not be resolved by the MUP. I was talking about Bosnia and Herzegovina, not about Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that under the circumstances and especially in early 1992 when you were faced with the breakup of Bosnia-Herzegovina and mounting tensions, the MUP could not do more than they could do during that period while you were in office in the MUP. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the MUP could, and I'm sorry that we didn't. I'm sorry that we did not arrest the members of the Presidency, the government, and the assembly. I'm sorry that we did not stage a coupe and give the people an opportunity to state their will. I'm sorry I didn't do that, because I didn't do it because it would have been misconstrued. I was not power-thirsty. All I wanted was for my former state to be the state with a rule of law, for the laws to be implemented. However, I put myself in a situation to have to confront those who thought that they were the law. And that is why many of my colleagues asked me how come I had not arrested all the Presidency members? How come I had not given the people to -- an opportunity to state their will? At that moment, it would have been the craziest of ideas. God know how I would have ended. In any case, I would not have been able to testify here today. That's the first reason. And the second reason was that I was not at all interested in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zepinic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot to tender into evidence 2D030381. The document has been translated. It is the information about the criminal activity of Veljko Milinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked or -- or -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D41, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before counsel for Stanisic cross-examines. Mr. Zepinic gave evidence on Thursday that he had listened to an intercept of a conversation between Zupljanin and Karadzic, and that he recognised the voice of Zupljanin from his dealings with him. There's been no cross-examination on that, so can we take it there is no dispute was indeed Mr. Zupljanin's voice that the witness heard on the intercept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the time being our position is identical to the position of Mr. Zecevic. We contest all the intercepted conversations for the reasons that have been already been put forth by my learned friend Mr. Zecevic. Neither I nor my client had an opportunity to listen to the audiotapes, although they have been disclosed to us, so I can't confirm this fact. I adhere to my position that -- and I would like to defer my final position on the entirety of the intercepted conversations to a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the short answer to what are you now saying is that, of course, the Chamber has made a ruling. But I come back to ask Ms. Korner, could you remind me as to what -- was it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was, Your Honour. It's P887. And, Your Honour, it is a different story. That's a different matter, whether or not, at the end of cross-examination of any witnesses who may deal with the actual recording and the like, that is one matter. But this witness has given clear evidence that he recognises, and I emphasise, recognises the voice. If the accused has not had an opportunity to listen to this, or to read it - which surprises me, because it was uploaded into e-court, we said we were going to do it, he must remember the conversation - then he should do it before the witness leaves. Because, Your Honours, it is important. This -- of course, is evidence which goes directly to whether or not the voice on it is -- is that of -- of Mr. Zupljanin. And I said this all along. It is clearly an important matter. And if there is it an issue, then it has to be put to the witness. This is it not something -- the obligation to put your case relating to important matters is a strict one. It is not good enough to say we haven't listened to it, and our position is we dispute everything on intercepts. This the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be heard on the matter, Your Honours, if it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that Ms. Korner, with all due respect, remark is unfounded. We have the ruling, which is very explicit. Either the witness is a party or is present. Now, if the witness says -- like in this case, I recognise the voice. As I said previously, he might recognise the voice, but it doesn't mean that the contents of the speech, of the conversation between the two are such as they are in the transcript. Therefore, it would be just a simple waste of time to cross-examine the witness. We ask the witness, does he -- does he know the contents of the -- of the -- of this particular conversation? He says he doesn't. That is why it was offered for MFI in -- in accordance with your -- with your ruling, Your Honours. I mean, if we -- if we are supposed to ask the witness to confirm that he recognised the other voice, I don't see what would be the point except loss of time, with no -- with no particular reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
