utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, that is not right. It does make a difference. And, Your Honour, leaving aside the content, nobody is suggesting that should have to be dealt with, but the voice recognition, I emphasise recognition, if it is disputed that this is the voice of Zupljanin, then that's a different matter. We have to call other evidence. If it is not disputed, then we don't have to. So it is not a waste of time. May I say, I will be saying exactly the same about the conversations with Stanisic. The content is one other matter, you know, whether they have been interfered with or whatever. But the voice -- that the witness can say, I recognise the voice is clearly important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Ms. Korner, hasn't the Chamber ruled that that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... No, you have not Your Honours. You have ruled that we cannot have it admitted if he was not a party to the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Or was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, or was present. But that is completely different, Your Honour. We are entitled to know now, as soon as we deal with this, whether or not there is a dispute, whatever the content may be, that this is the voice of Zupljanin or Stanisic. You cannot keep your powder dry forever. This is an important part of the evidence, and we say you're obliged under the Rules and under the ruling in the case of Brdjanin to put your case. Do you accept this is the voice of Zupljanin and, later on, Stanisic or not? It has nothing whatsoever to do as to whether the content has been interfered with in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you remind us, Mr. Krgovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just like Mr. Zecevic our Defence has realised that the intercepts have been MFI'd until further corroboration. And that's why I understood that I'm not supposed to question the witnesses about the intercepts. I can, but, the way I understood it, I did not include it in my cross-examination. In any case, I can ask the witness about all that, and I can spend about half an hour on that. But I don't think it will be of any assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I'm sorry, this is beating around the bush. The question that was put to you was: Do you accept that the voice heard on this particular intercept is the voice of your client? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, how can you say no, if you say you haven't listened to it? I'm sorry, Your Honours, that is simply not good enough. This is a "no" simply said to Your Honours in answer to the question. Cannot be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. Our position is as follows. From the very beginning, when it comes to the intercepts, we believed that they are not illegal, that they have not been taken in an illegal way, that a context has not been established, that the identity of the participants has not been established in a proper way. The Prosecutor is taking shortcuts, and we do not accept their suggestions. The first one that the voice indeed belongs to Stojan Zupljanin, and we also dispute the context. I believe that the two facets of that same issue should go together and that they should not be separated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, what I'm trying to avoid is going back over ground which is fully covered and in respect of which we have ruled. In summary, what the position of the Prosecution is, is that when the witness was led on -- when evidence is led from the witness on this point in respect of this particular item he says that he recognised the voice as of that Zupljanin. The -- your inability to challenge that evidence, that positive evidence which the witness gave, is, as I understand it, based on the fact that the -- you, with the assistance of your client of course, have not had an opportunity to yourselves to have heard the transcript -- to have heard the intercept. The -- and the -- I don't know what your position is in terms of the transcript of the -- of the intercept. But the position of the Prosecution is that the document, having been marked for identification on the basis that there was this challenge to -- is really a question of weight, not admissibility. The result would be if you failed to go further, that the document would -- the condition which would have been imposed by the -- only having been marked for identification would then disappear. I think that that's a fair summary of the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I explain. There is evidence before the Court that, whether or not the -- the intercept is actually fully admitted after you have heard about its provenance and so forth, that the voice on it is that of Stojan Zupljanin. That is clearly an important matter. Because it goes to all -- it corroborates the identification which may be made in the future by the person who recorded it, which we have dealt with, which Judge Harhoff related to. It is therefore important evidence. That evidence is now before the Court. If it is later to be challenged, when, and if, Zupljanin were to give evidence, then it would be quite wrong that it had not been put to this witness who has given positive affirmative evidence, and that is the purpose of the rule that one must put the case. Otherwise, it would entail getting Dr. Zepinic back again. And that is why it has put. And Mr. Krgovic is simply saying this for the sake of saying this. If what he is saying is correct, that neither he nor his client have actually listened to the intercept, there is no problem by that. In the next adjournment, we have got them all on CD; we can get him; he can listen to it. What I'm asking Your Honours to do is make a ruling that, it is so important, if it is disputed it must be put at this stage. That's the ruling I'm asking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We can actually play the intercept straightaway. We've got it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm not sure I understand. Are you proposing to actually play the intercept in Court?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, so that, Your Honours, there can be no problem about Mr. Zupljanin hearing his voice, so he doesn't have to wait for the adjournment. We can play it right now. And then we can have whether or not this is his voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Ms. Korner, the Chamber is of the view that even if that were done, it cannot compel the Defence to answer the question as to whether they accept that it is the voice of Zupljanin or not, because that would be to -- that would, in essence, require them to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Reveal their hand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Not merely reveal their hand, but to incriminate the -- the accused Zupljanin, which would be a clear violation of all the principles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest of respect, that simply is not right. They are obliged, if they don't agree with what is being said, to put what is their case. What is the Defence case? There has been evidence now given by, as I put -- as I said earlier, a far more qualified witness than any of -- any of the technicians or whatever to dealt with this. That -- that's the point of putting a case. It is not incriminating your client; it is it whether it is disputed. We had this argument. That's what the whole appeal is about in the case of Brdjanin. The case against Brdjanin was that he went on the radio and made inflammatory statements against non-Serbs. And we -- we got to the position where a witness gave evidence of those inflammatory statements; it was not challenged by Mr. Ackerman who was defending Brdjanin. And I asked the same question. I said, Is it disputed that he made those statements? Yes, it is, said Ackerman, but I'm not going to put it, I don't have to. And that's why that case went to appeal, and that's the authority. So now we have clear evidence this is the voice of Zupljanin. If it is disputed -- and this is an good reason for this, Your Honour, because if is disputed that it is his voice, leaving aside whether there has been any inference with it, we have to call a great deal of more evidence. And that's why the Defence cannot sit on what is their Defence - indeed they should have said all of this in their pre-trial brief but didn't - whether it is accepted that's his voice. It is not incriminating his client. It is it putting a proper case. This is the Defence case: We do not agree this is his voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Zecevic, let me finish. They're saying we don't -- at the moment Mr. Krgovic is saying I don't know one way or another whether it is his voice or not. But if he is actually going to say having heard this, or if that is their case, that is not even the voice of Mr. Zupljanin, there is an grave mistake, and Dr. Zepinic has made a grave mistake in identifying it, then that is something that we are entitled to know right now because it reflects on evidence we have to call. It is one of the reasons why there is an obligation to put your case. I cannot make it any clearer than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, I'll try and be very concise and very brief. There is a significant difference between the Brdjanin and Zupljanin case because we're talking about a show that was aired on the radio; whereas, here, we're talking about the intercepts. We claim and our position is clear that those were illegal listening-in exercises which were not allowed under the law. Therefore, there could be no parallel between the Brdjanin case and the ruling in the Brdjanin case and this situation. I really understand Ms. Korner's desire. However, at the end of the day, she is only interested in the contents of the transcript of the intercept in question. This is her primary interest. Of course, she is interested in finding out that that was, indeed, a conversation between the two individuals. However, the essence of the matter lies in the transcript itself. Therefore, I really believe that it was a waste of time if we are put in a position to question every witness and ask them to recognise the voice of the participants. Needless to say, they are not qualified to recognise or to engage in voice recognition exercises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the Chamber having ruled on the question of legality, it's only issue of contents that remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, I'm just trying to put things in a context and tell you what the position of the Defence has been from the very start of this case. That's why I mentioned this, but I'm fully aware of the ruling made by this Trial Chamber. There is nothing in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the representations of counsel from both sides and essentially has decided not to revisit the ruling that it has already made. We fully understand the logic and, if I may so, immanently sensible position which the Prosecution has taken but if the -- for tactical reasons, the Defence chooses not to show their hand at this point, Then, of course, certain consequences will follow for both sides. But the Chamber will not revisit the ruling that it gave last week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, I'm asking you this now on record. It is your ruling that there is no obligation for the Defence to put its case on the voice recognition by this witness of both accused on tape?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would prefer to phrase it the way we have done it, rather than accepting your -- adopting your formulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'm asking -- because I'm asking for, obviously -- can I make it clear, I consider this to be a matter of such importance I'm asking for a clear ruling that we can, if necessary, ask for an appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the ruling that we have made is that the identity of a person who speaks in an intercept can be verified by the interceptor; or can be verified by a witness, if that witness was himself a party to the conversation, or was present in the room when the conversation took place. So the short answer to your point is that we do not believe that Mr. Zepinic, as much as he may be able to recognise the voice, and as much as we also think that it would be very helpful if the Defence would agree to that, that Mr. Zepinic is not the appropriate witness to certify the identity of Mr. Zupljanin's voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that was your ruling, and I was prepared to leave that ruling, as it was. But this is a different aspect, and it's a different ruling. If your ruling is that there is no obligation as -- I'm sorry I just need to go back to the words that were used. If for tactical -- you are ruling, that the Defence are entitled, to, for tactical reasons not to put what its case is on what is a vital part of our case. That's why I have asked for a clear ruling, Your Honours, because we say, with the greatest respect, that cannot be right and is not within the Rules. There comes a point which, as I say, should have taken place at the pre-trial brief stage, by the Defence, where they have their obligation to put their case and cannot, for tactical reasons, refrain. This is such a case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But then I said earlier, Mr. Korner, if I might interrupt, that rather than adopting your formulation, the Chamber would choose its own language. We are not ruling as broadly, as you represented, that the tactical reasons the Defence has no obligation just to indicate its case. Clearly we would not rule that. What we have said is that in this specific issue of whether the Defence has to disclose its position on the positive evidence of this witness in which he says he recognises the voice of Zupljanin on the tape, the Chamber will not require the Defence to do so. The Defence must -- and that is why I used the word tactical. The Defence must presumably know why it is running its case in the way this it is. There are, of course, with everything in life, consequences that follow from such decisions as are taken. But the very narrow ruling of the -- of the Chamber on this, is that the Chamber, in its view, cannot require the Defence to so answer the question as put by the Prosecution. It's as narrow as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are no consequences because as I remarked yesterday or -- not yesterday, there is no ability to -- to make a wasted cost order against the Defence. The logical progression from this ruling is, as we don't know one way or another whether if and when the defendant gave -- the accused gave evidence they would accept it was their voices, we will have to instruct people, experts to make voice identifications which will be identifications done by experts which costs an enormous amount of money because we don't know what the Defence is, and you won't order them to put it. It is it simple as that. The waste of money is fantastic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, our ruling says that this witness cannot certify the voice of any accused in -- in the case we're talking, now, he was not present, et cetera, et cetera. So what -- what would the Defence have to answer to? He cannot -- he says he recognises, but we ruled he cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, how can he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that finishes the business.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, it doesn't, Your Honour, because it is still evidence, because I asked about that when you made this ruling. I see Mr. Zecevic is standing. It would be preferable if he sat down and waited until I finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to indicate to the Trial Chamber that I have something to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked whether I was prohibited from asking the witness whether he recognised, and I underline and emphasise recognised, the voice, and I was told not. So in this case, there is evidence that this witness who knew Zupljanin for a number of years and even better new Stanisic recognises the voice. Now that is evidence which is admissible because you ruled it to be admissible; the weight that you give it is another matter. But clearly the weight is additionally added to it if it is not disputed that it is his voice. And it makes Dr. Zepinic in his recognition a more credible witness. That's why it is it important. It also, as I said before, corroborates whatever evidence, if it is accepted, we get relating to the actual recording. So it cannot be said that it is not relevant, admissible, important evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will say only the following so as not to use more time. I really consider it very unfair on the part of the OTP to accuse the Defence and everybody else of squandering money on experts and the like. The fact is the following. My client voluntarily agreed to an interview with the OTP. He was interviewed for six days and not one intercept was played to him. The OTP had its opportunity then to play all those intercepts, and Mr. Stanisic would have been in a position to reply to his questions because he had agreed to those interviews but not one intercept was shown to him, nor was he asked about them. So it is the right of any accused to remain silent. So I have nothing else to add. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Can I start, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm Slobodan Cvijetic, and I am a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mico Stanisic. Now it is my turn to ask some questions. Well, some is an understatement; there are going to be quite a few. But before I start asking questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, before you hit your stride, we have been informed by the Registry that we can sit until 5.30 today. So we would resume -- at 1.45, we would resume at 2.30 with a view to sitting until 5.30 with a suitable break somewhere in between that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, before I start asking you questions, I will just ask you, since we speak the same language, to follow the transcript, and once my question is recorded, start giving your answer. I know you speak English. I hope that you understand what I said.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to comply with your request, as best I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me first return to that part of the examination-in-chief that took place on Thursday and Friday, in order to clarify some things and thus enable the Chamber to understand how such an important part of the public administration as the MUP functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask the Registrar to show the -- to show Exhibit P875 to the witness. That is, to put it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could the Registry please inquire what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please enlarge the upper part, showing the first three persons, or the three highest ranking persons. All right, I believe that this will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, here you see the organisational structure of the MUP, and we can see what it looks like. At the head of the ministry there is the minister, Mr. Delimustafic, followed by yourself and Mr. Mico Stanisic to the left and the right respectively. This is the moment when Mr. Stanisic was an advisor to the minister for national security. That I believe was the exact official title that will he had.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether that's the exact name, but, yes, he was an advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. In this hierarchy of the MUP, you will agree with me when I say that, if Mr. Delimustafic was the number one man, you would have been the number two man?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But then you will agree that Mr. Stanisic, at least graphically, shouldn't be at the same level with you, because in the MUP hierarchy there is no vertical line down from him in the hierarchy and in the command of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who made this schematic. Apart from Mr. Stanisic there were two more advisors in the MUP. It wasn't just Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But have you listened to my question? But do you agree with what I said, what I put to you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That, in the MUP hierarchy, Mr. Stanisic, as an advisor, doesn't have a vertical line down from his position, so he doesn't -- he doesn't have subordinates in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right, you agree. Let me put it this way. His position and his authority starts and ends inside the minister's office. Basically the minister and him depend on each other.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the minister depends on both of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you agree, basically, with the rest of what I said. He is in the minister's office?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, speaking about which, can you please state the names of the other advisors.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Krizanovic, but now, frankly I can't remember the name of the financial advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I believe that we have explained this, and you will agree that possibly in this schematic, his position should probably have been depicted differently?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that statement. I think that Mr. Stanisic's position should not have been depicted here at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, because it's specific. He was an advisor in the minister's office.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's what I was trying to say. The point is that he is absent from the organisational structure of the MUP, and obviously we agree about that. Thank you. My next question follows from -- follows up on some of your answers provided to the OTP. And before I put that question to you, I'll ask the usher to hand this binder to you. The -- this is evidence I'm about to show you, so you'll have hard copies, and we don't have to look at the screens. Please go directly to tab 2 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We'll use that later. Just put it down for the time being. It isn't numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: 1D011054 is the reference for the Chamber. While the Registrar is looking for that, I'll just say that is the Law on Internal Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's the expurged version. Am I being signalled that it is time for a break? Right, Mr. Zepinic, we'll break off here and continue right where we broke off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope Ms. Korner is not proofing the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I was distracted by something that happened outside court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, please proceed continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Let's just wait for the witness to get ready.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us now try to clarify another topic, namely, the position to which Mr. Stanisic was appointed and you signed the decision, you said, while he was at the city secretariat of the interior of Sarajevo. In your statement, that is in one sentence, that you uttered in replying to a question, you mentioned two positions of his. You said that he was the chief of the CSB or -- and then you say he was the chief of the city SUP. So let me ask you now to go to Article 26, paragraph 2 of the law you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, I believe that's on page 7. In the B/C/S version, it's Article 26, paragraph 2. I hope both versions are aligned or -- well, these are both the B/C/S versions. Let us display the English version for the Chamber. All right now. Let us see how the law regulates that, then we will have no problems. So the law distinguishes between these two organisational forms. One is the CSB of Sarajevo; that is one thing. And the other thing is the secretariat of the interior of the city of Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So let us try and distinguish this from now on. So Mr. Stanisic was the secretary of the secretariat of the interior of the city of Sarajevo. Isn't that correct? And that's what the decision you signed reads?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the decision reads.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the answer of the witness because of the background noise produced by Mr. Cvijetic with shuffling through the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, the interpreters are having difficulty from the background noise from your papers. So if you could -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not switch off the microphone. We'll find the decision so we know what the law stipulates.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And let's now find your decision under which number it can be found. We put it back on the screen too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P888 is the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And in your binder, Mr. Zepinic, It's number 56. At the very end. I believe we'll come to terms about that very soon. Once read your own decision, please read out what the decision is called.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretary to the SUP of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must distinguish the secretary to the SUP of the city of Sarajevo and the secretary of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We must distinguish the chief of the CSB of Banja Luka from the secretary of the SUP of the city of Banja Luka. Likewise, we must distinguish between the chief of the SUP of Sarajevo, which covers also Romanija, and the city SUP of Sarajevo. If you ask me who the secretary in the city SUP of Sarajevo was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then I will read out to you the names of persons in the respective positions. The chief of the CSB of Sarajevo was Kemo Sabovic. And Mr. Stanisic was secretary -- at the secretariat of the interior of Sarajevo as an organisational unit of the SJB -- sorry, CSB, and in line with the law.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do we agree now?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then we are saying things that aren't provided for by the law. I'll put the following to you. This may explain the situation. Before Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Zeljko Iljic was in that position, and after him there was Mr. Kijac [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, sir, can you not expect me to remember all the names and all positions of the MUP and when Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Kemo Sabovic replaced somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I had expected that we would clarify this, but the Chamber will interpret the regulations because in the regulations I can see two organisational structures and two persons in two different positions. But if you cannot help us, let's proceed. Do tell me now that we're speaking about the SUP of Sarajevo or, as you say, the city of Sarajevo, tell us, within whose purview was securing large gatherings, political order, such as the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, party rallies or conferences, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the purview of the Ministry of the Interior, and the ministry decided in accordance with its regulations that the chief of the municipal secretariats to provide security for the facilities in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the occasion with some incident involving Mrs. Ostojic an order to the city SUP followed to provide security to some personalities from political life such as Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Karadzic, et cetera. Do you remember that may have been your order?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I cannot be sure whether it was or wasn't. But it was certainly an order that was passed on from the ministry to our subordinate structures to carry out some tasks that involved providing security to facilities and persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's call that lower organisational level the city SUP.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or to police stations in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on to the third topic. So we're still dealing with the same law. So if you wouldn't mind, let's look at Article 36 and Article 37. Let me see where that is in the English translation. It's the same document. Or, actually, you're right, we must return to 1D011054. That is the law. I apologise. I forgot that I called up another exhibit. All right. In the English version, this is on pages 10 and 11, and in the B/C/S version the Articles are 36 and 37. I believe that this is it in both linguistic versions, but possibly they should be enlarged. If you don't mind, Mr. Zepinic, do read these two Articles but you may know them anyway.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Articles?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: 36 and 37. The law stipulates two types of units you spoke about. With other professionals from your line of business, we discussed this and checked it. So -- and we found out that Article 36 covers the Special Police brigade. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Because the nature of the duties and tasks under Article 33, appropriate police units shall be established for the purpose within the Republican Secretariat."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that should be the spot. So does this cover the special brigade?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This refers to any police unit, including traffic police, but also unit providing security to persons and facilities including Special Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Article 37 states that so-called PJP, that is special units, ad hoc units, can be established. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a possibility for -- for establishing such units in case of need.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the essence of my question, and you can see that in the law also, that it was the exclusive right of the minister to establish such units and appoint their commanders.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This reads the Republican Secretary. That's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. You are right; it says the Republican Secretary, because this is the old law in which the old terminology can be found. Mr. Zepinic, can you find where the law refers to any other type of unit or any other person with the authority to establish such a type of police units, in the law?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer this question, I would have to be a lawyer, which I'm not. And, secondly, you should have given me the document in advance for me to read it through thoroughly and familiarise myself with it. But if the Chamber wants me to do so, I can read this for a couple of hours and then I will be able to answer such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's go on. We'll call specialists for laws and regulations who can then interpret this for us. The next thing I wanted to deal with is the relationship that existed between the MUP and the Presidency, or the cabinet respectively. In a situation of the imminent threat of war or in a state of war, can you tell me what the respective strengths of the Presidency or the cabinet were in relation to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean who was number one and who was number two?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, number one is the Presidency, and number two is the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that the Presidency could even directly speak to the minister.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Translation is not correct. The number one is Presidency, and number two is the cabinet. I would say government.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry for intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. The Presidency, in some cases, had the right to deal directly with the minister with -- about security-related issues?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me now move on to a question that was put to you, and when you spoke about the rhetoric of ethnic leaders or leaders of ethnically based parties. To be more specific it was a question of the rhetoric used by Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, just one moment, please, something wrong with the record. What is said after the intervention of the witness, because what he said was not correct. Is exactly the same as what he said before. Well, number one is the Presidency, and number two is the cabinet. And then the witness says, No, that is not correct. And now re-read the number one is the Presidency, and the number two is the cabinet. It is exactly the same. So let's -- let's have that right of what the witness wants -- the difference with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, I believe the witness was having -- taking an issue with the interpretation of he said Vlada, and it was interpreted as cabinet, and he said government. But cabinet and government are basically the same thing. That's -- that was the intervention as I -- I understand stood the witness to be.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the judge, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but that is not the same thing. Sorry, Mr. Zecevic, it's not the same. [In English] Cabinets or prime minister is something different than the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you meant --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say -- sorry for intervention again. I would say number one was the Presidency, and number two was the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. That was the essence of the question, and I don't want to go into terminological issues such as cabinet or government. You -- we spoke about the rhetoric of ethnic leaders, the specific question asked of you was about the rhetoric of Mr. Karadzic. You will agree with me, won't you, Mr. Zepinic, that such nationalist rhetoric was also used by the leaders of other ethnically-based parties, namely the SDA, and the HDZ. Am I right, especially in the election campaign?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you listen to me attentively on Thursday and Friday, I said that this applies to all ethnic leaders. Specifically this was about Dr. Karadzic, but the language used didn't differ when it comes to other ethnic leaders either. They swore less frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me when I say that, with this ethnically-centred or nationalist rhetoric Mr. Izetbegovic, at least officially, started with the Islamic declaration but which you, as a police officer, certainly know.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Islamic declaration is something I know from the time when Mr. Izetbegovic was sentenced for nationalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. It has been admitted into evidence already, and I won't quote that declaration anymore because historians have already commented it. But let me ask you whether you, as a police officer, know that it was reprinted at the beginning of the election campaign in 1990, that it was part of the party programme of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must correct you, I'm not a police officer. And secondly, if you ask me about the first printing of the Islamic declaration, then I can say that it was printed in Belgrade for the campaign of Mr. Izetbegovic which was micro-nationalism. Mr. Seselj and Mr. Cosic were the greatest opponents to the Prosecution of Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Give me an opportunity to explain, because the question is regarding second publishing Islamic declaration written by Mr. Izetbegovic. I have no recollection, and I have no evidence about such declaration being published or not. It wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you have, actually, answered my question. Just please focus on what I ask you. Can you agree with me when I say that the Croats, too, had their nationalist rhetoric and that they put that into practice by establishing the HZHB?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you for one reason. You're mentioning a Herzegovinian Croatian party established by Mr. Mate Boban, if I remember will, in March 1990. That party or that entity was part of the Croatian Democratic Union from Zagreb. That department, probably reinforced by the efforts of Mr. Susak and others from the Western Herzegovina, in August 1990 it changed its name to Croatian Democratic Union, and for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and its president elected was Dr. Davor Petrinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I would then show you the document relating to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna when we get there. Let me first show you a video-clip that was used in examination-in-chief the exhibit number is 1D108, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry, I made a mistake. I think it has a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's the Death of Yugoslavia. It's -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We found it. P907.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to the uniformed persons, the persons in uniform that will appear there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: THE NARRATOR: "But he didn't know it would start from his own side. It happened as the guests arrived at a Serb wedding. A Muslim killed the father of the groom. That night, Serbs hit back.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Hands up. Come here. THE NARRATOR: "The gunmen erected armed barricades all over the Bosnian capital.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] It's just a chisel, mate. The Serbs of Sarajevo demand, number one, that the Bosnian government unconditionally put an end to all efforts seeking international recognition."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, stop it here, please. Can you recognise who this is?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the face, but this is a paramilitary belonging to the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the persons, I cannot identify them. I can't. I really cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll stop it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As a police officer, did you have a chance to meet Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never met Juka Prazina in my life. It is it another story that he incarcerated me when the war started, but I never met him in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But did you meet him when he incarcerated you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Then our argument that one of the persons seen in the video is him cannot be confirmed by you.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But what can you tell us about him? Who is he? What was he?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a pre-war criminal, who, very soon, became the commander of paramilitary units in Sarajevo, and, as far as I know, he was one of the first to be appointed general in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he gathered around him a company of criminals. They divided the town among them, and within three days they very efficiently robbed all food in Sarajevo and stores, cars. They even stole a -- the chair from a friend -- a friend of mine's barbershop in Sarajevo. So they went about robbing and looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you know that under his control one of the unofficial prisons were founded?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that prison was under the control of Juka Prazina. But I know that there were a number of private prisons around Sarajevo and that anybody and their uncle could open them, and they did. And those prisons were not only for the Serbs but also for those who did not agree with the concept of crimes that were launched immediately after -- at the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. As we're talking about the barricades, the footage started with the incident involving the murder of two members of a Serbian wedding party. As far as I know, the perpetrators were immediately identified, arrested, and immediately released. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct that they were immediately released. The Ministry of the Interior identified the perpetrators, it arrested them, they were remanded into custody for as long as they could be remanded, as can be confirmed by Messrs. Zupljanin and Stanisic. We were only allowed to keep them for three days, and we sent the criminal report to the Prosecutor's office for Bosnia-Herzegovina for further proceedings. I don't know why Mr. Kovac, who was the public Prosecutor at the time, rejected our report. You should ask him. As far as the security services, everything was done professionally and under the law. When it came to the perpetrators of those murders, they were indeed brought in and kept for as long as we could keep them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is it true that during the interviews they said that they had done what they did and pursuant to the instructions from the office of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed about that by the investigators that Mr. Delic, also known as Celo, who was one of the persons who had stated that the order arrived from the office of Mr. Izetbegovic and the -- he followed that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now just one more question before I move on, a question of -- with regard to the incidents that happened during that time. Just briefly, do you know anything about the attacks against the army, and did you personally intervene in some situations? And I mean Grude and other such instances. Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who were the perpetrators of those attacks.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attacks were perpetrated against the column of military vehicles, and it was carried out by paramilitary units and paramilitaries in certain locations and areas. That happened in the Neretva Valley predominantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Who were those paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those paramilitaries were composed of various criminal groups, similar to Mr. Milinkovic in the Banja Luka region. And if you're asking me, their main purpose was not ethnically based. They were primarily criminals, and they used every opportunity to tip the security situation in the area by launching attacks against military facilities, police stations, not only in western Herzegovina but all over Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The crime in Sijekovac dates back to that very early period. Is it true that the Special Police brigade returned from that area or ordered to return from that area and that the Croats did not allow them to intervene?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, that's not true. I did not allow the Special Police unit to go in and intervene in Sijekovac for a simple reason. At the previous government session we had considered the possibility. I apologise, it was an extended session of the Presidency and the government. There was a request for the Special Police units to intervene and to take over the role of a buffer zone. I will tell you what I replied to Mr. Izetbegovic on that occasion. I told him that every buffer, once it returns, is stained with blood. I believe that the situation in Sijekovac had to be dealt with in political ways and not by way of the intervention launched by a Special Police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now just a very brief question. Who perpetrated the crime?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The crime in Sijekovac?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it with a was a group led by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is it impossible to hear the witness because of the shuffling of the papers coming from the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, please remember to turn off your microphone because they are picking up your papers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the leader of the paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, what was the name of the leader of the paramilitary group that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it was Armin Pohara. I know his name, because he was a president of Green Party.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Cvijetic please switch off his microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in early 1990s. [Interpretation] At the time when his deputy was Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Which units he belonged to when he carried out attack on Sijekovac?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I don't know. I know that the ministry established a commission to carry out an investigation with regard to that murder and the massacre. Not only murders but a veritable massacre committed against the civilian population of Sijekovac. As far as I know, I apologise if I'm mistaken, I believe that a police officer also got killed in at that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on to the following document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just see whether it already has a number. The document is P885.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your tab it is document under -- in your binder, it is document under tab 57.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You've already seen the document. You saw it during the examination-in-chief. It is an intercept of a conversation. Could you please look at page 3 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try and locate the corresponding English page. We need page 4 in B/C/S. The following page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's just see -- this is a text. Look at the lower part where Mr. Karadzic says: "I spoke to them, and I calmed them down." And now I need a corresponding section in the English version. I believe it is on page 5; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you see that? The document has already been shown to you, as I have already said. And you said, on the 28th of January, on page 573, you put this conversation in a context, and you identified the voice of Mico Stanisic. Could you please read both paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you. You have to look carefully, to see whether I indeed said that I had recognised Mr. Stanisic or I said that I assumed that it could be Mr. Stanisic. We're talking about two entirely different things. He does mention a Mico. I don't know which Mico is in question. I didn't state that for a fact, so check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you read what it says here?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking because you said that you allow for the possibility that that was indeed Mr. Stanisic. However, let's just agree on one thing. It transpired from the second part of Karadzic's conversation with yourself that the person was an MP in the assembly who was also a member of the council of municipalities, and if he was removed somebody else would be given his position, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I don't know whether that person was indeed Mico Stanisic or somebody else. And I have already stated that several times. I don't know whether Stanisic was a member of the SDS party at the time, and whether he was an MP in the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was put to him that he identified the voice of Stanisic; no, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not correct, not correct, Your Honours. I'm putting it to the witness that, based on the nickname Mico he allowed for the possibility that that person was indeed Mico Stanisic. We never heard the voice of the alleged Mico.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate that. In the question he put at page 78, something -- the line has gone up now. He said: "You identified the voice of Mr. Stanisic." No, he didn't. 78, line 19. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sure that the interpretation was wrong. I didn't use the term "voice." We never listened to the recording; there is no way I could have used the word "voice."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, therefore, that identification based on nicknames is something that one has to be cautious about.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I stated. It was just my assumption. It was not a definite identification of Mr. Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on to a different topic. But before I do that, you asked me about a document that is separate in the first group of documents. And let me ask you this. Namely, this is 1D108, when you were talking about -- let's just see it on the screen. And can we immediately move to the second page in the B/C/S version, which is immediately after the page that is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 2 immediately. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And I assume that it would be the second page in the English version. But if not, then we'll manage with what we have. The bottom part says that the Presidency established a Crisis Staff. I believe that ... yes, now we have the correct pages. You were telling us about your attempts to intervene with regard to the barricades, and you claimed -- and you told us who had you called with this regard, and they referred to Mr. Ejub Ganic, and they told you about him, that he was in charge on behalf of the Presidency of such situations, if I understood you probably?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read the paragraph starting with the words: "The Presidency establishes a Crisis Staff ..."

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Slow down, please. The question is this: Do you know that Mr. Ganic was, as it says here, the coordinator on behalf of the Crisis Staff of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for this kind of situations? Let's see if your answer has been recorded. And the question -- now your answer has not been recorded. Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The answer could not be heard because the speakers were overlapping again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, we never heard your answer to the question that was put to you. Did you know about Ganic's role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was aware of the fact that Mr. Ganic had a been appointed as the coordinator on behalf of the Crisis Staff of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, sir. And again to both counsels, please be careful not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question with this regard is as follows. Your attempts to find him that day failed, although he was supposedly in charge of such situations.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now I would like to move on to a different topic, the one that started your examination-in-chief. Let's first go to a regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just been suggested to ask you what day was it when you were looking for him, the day when the barricades were erected.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was looking for him on the day when the barricades had been erected, but I failed. He arrived at the Presidency on the following day, and at my proposal he was removed as the coordinator on behalf of the Crisis Staff of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Cvijetic, can you explain to us the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am dealing with the topics raised during the examination-in-chief. During the examination-in-chief, he took some time talking about the barricades and his roles in dealing with the situation, and he also told us who he had called and what the reactions were on behalf of those who he had called. And within that context, he said that he was also referred to Mr. Ganic and that Mr. Ganic played a certain role when it came to dealing with such situations. I only showed him a document and asked him to confirm that that was, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But he did confirm that during his examination-in-chief, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But he did not confirm nor was he ever asked what his official role had been, and I established that through this document, and the witness confirmed what the role of Mr. Ganic was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. Mr. Cvijetic, how is that relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the Crisis Staff of the Presidency, which dates back to September 1991, Your Honours. And the main task of the coordinator of that Crisis Staff was what the witness was talking about at great length. And that Crisis Staff and that coordinator did not deliver, they did not perform their duty, as has been confirmed by the witness. And which complements our thesis that Crisis Staffs existed and functioned even before the Serbian Democratic Party established them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think there is a misunderstanding here. This was a discussion about the SDS Crisis Staff on the barricades. Nothing to do with whatever Mr. Cvijetic thinks it was, in-chief anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is up to you be the judge of that. We have our own thesis, and we want to support it because we believe that it is relevant to establish when Crisis Staffs were first established as organisations and forms of functioning. We have proved that they existed in September 1991 and witness confirmed their existence, and he also shed light on the function and role of Mr. Ejub Ganic at the time. And this is exactly what we have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would appreciate if you simply could put the questions relating to these matters to the witness head on. But, in any case, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, let's first see this piece of regulation, 1D004042. This is a Law on General People's Defence [as interpreted], which is a topic which you already discussed in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 61 in the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And in your binder, sir, it will be under tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just an intervention of transcript, Your Honours. 83, line 17, it is All People's Defence. I believe that is what Mr. Cvijetic's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian version, we are on Article 91, and the English version we are on page 61. We're looking for Article 91. What matters is to have the English version, and the two of us speak Serbian so we can make do. Can you please open your B/C/S version on page 3 where you will find Article 91 -- or, rather, the document is under tab 3. Look for Article 91. Do you have it? Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. We're dealing with armed forces: "The armed force make up a single entity and are comprised of a Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence." Would you agree with me that this is the shortest possible and the simplest definition of the armed forces within the system of All People's Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a legal expert, so I can't say either yes or no. This is the 1982 law, as far as I know. I don't know whether there were any amendments or new laws after that, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We're dealing with the federal law which was applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that in the legal definition of the armed forces, the police or the Ministry of the Interior does not feature as an integral part of the armed forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right, yes, I agree with you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now let's move to page 67 in the English version. And for you, sir, could you please turn your pages to Article 104. 104. Do you see this Article 104, in it does envisage a possibility to engage police forces in combat. But if that the case, the police forces are resubordinated to the military commander to whose area they are deployed.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You have already explained to us -- that to us during your examination-in-chief. This means that the competent commander of a corps can issue a written order or a -- an oral order in threat of war and ask for a certain number of police officers to be placed at his disposal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At the moment when they arrive in the area of his responsibility, their official competencies of civilian police officers are abolished. They become part of the military bodies. They are resubordinated to a military commander, and they are held responsible just like any other member of the military. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And if that happens your authority over them ceases to exist?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You have to say no. Could you please repeat your answer? And let me repeat my question. Do you still have any authority over that group of policemen in a situation like that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In such a situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we have been through this a number of times, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will then continue with my following question, because the witness was asked about the circumstances in the examination-in-chief. Let me just verify that, nothing more. Here is a high-ranking police officer, Your Honours, we will not have the opportunity or indeed the need to ask anybody of a lower rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So my final question about this Article --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I have just one intervention, sorry. "Here is a high-ranking police officer." I told you already I wasn't police officer, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So if in such a situation when they are resubordinated, I'm speaking about former civilian police officers, if they commit a war crime or any crime, they are then prosecuted before a military tribunal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now your answer has been recorded. It's okay. Why have I brought up this law? On pages 114 and 115 of the English version, more specifically, Article 207 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 114, 115, so the Article is 207.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you read Article 207 in the meantime, sir?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You know this from the system, Mr. Zepinic. It stipulates that all -- everybody in the country is obliged to make -- to prepare for defence, make plans and even establish staffs, et cetera. These preparations comprised all institutions in the state, including the MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the 1982 act, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then I will show you some documents signed by you to check their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see documents 1D159, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your binder, that is number 6. Mr. Zepinic, take a look at this document. Can you recognise one of your own documents? Do you just confirm that this is a practical implementation of what we have just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, then tell me.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You, Mr. Cvijetic, are trying to apply the 1982 act to the newly-created circumstances after the multi-party elections held in 1990. This law that you have placed in front of me was passed in a country with a single-party system which was ruled by the League of Communists. At the time when I was in authority, there was a coalition of ethnic parties, based on the decision of the Assemblies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, taken in January 1991, that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, political pluralism should be developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But my sweep wasn't so broad.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Cvijetic. Your Honour. Because you are trying to implement in something what is totally inadequate regarding document in time when we had totally different political situation than on time that political party formed government, Presidency, and cabinet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's your permission, I will explain further. You asking me here about organisation. Of military organisation -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Zepinic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [No interpretation] [Interpretation] You're asking me about the conditions in an imminent threat of war, a state of war, in a crisis, and I ask you who in Bosnia-Herzegovina decided that there was an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just one question. Is this your document?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now that you are unwilling to comment it, it has been exhibited already. Let's continue. Do you recognise the following document, document number 7 -- well, but let's not go into this. Let me just, by way of finishing, ask you in general about the situation. The defence preparations of the organs of the -- in the interior also include drafting plans, the establishing of staffs, but exclusively for the carrying out of police duties in the newly arisen, more difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, then I don't know what are we disagreeing about.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We disagree about the fact that nobody ever proclaimed the state of crisis or imminent threat of war or the state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, I'm referring to the obligation that even in peace such preparations must be conducted. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me when I say that, to that end, and because of the expected worsening of the security situation and operational staff can be established that will assist the minister in the implementation of his task in these new aggravated the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot reply with any degree of certainty that was indeed the case. But the ministry or -- minister or his office were duty-bound to establish a team that would vouch, say, the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said team or staff; right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Well, we can use such or terms or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: To confirm what we were saying, let us see document 1D030526. And you can find it at number 13. Let us just wait for the English version to appear. This is a document which wasn't signed by you but, rather, Mr. Avdo Hebib as the commander or the head of the staff. And he informs the other units that such an operation staff has been established. Is this a confirmation of what we have just spoken about?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: For what purpose exactly, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document confirms the conversation and the topic Mr. Zepinic and I discussed about the existence of an operational staff within the Ministry of the Interior in extraordinary circumstances, or in a crisis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but we disagree. The staff was established because the security situation had worsened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has identified the document, and I believe it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just remind you of the date of the document. It is dated 6 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your witness resigned a few days earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I suppose this document could be admitted. But wouldn't we just be adding paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We haven't had any document of this type so far, but I believe it is relevant for the positions of the Defence. It is relevant for us, and I believe it can assist the Trial Chamber to clarify some issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, as usual, we're not trying to prevent you from tendering evidence to us. On the contrary. But we need have to have a clear understanding of just how this will assist the Defence case, and thereby how it is relevant to this Trial Chamber. And I'm not sure I understand it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, then we should discuss that in the absence of the witness. I can explain to you why it is relevant to us, but this will take some time, I am afraid. I am willing to provide you an answer but in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are just up on a break, Mr. Cvijetic. Perhaps what the -- what could happen is that the witness could be excused a little ahead of us, and you could briefly explain how this is relevant. Mr. Zepinic, we will be taking a break shortly, and we would resume at 2.30 because we have an extended session today in order to complete your testimony. But the Court is not rising immediately so the usher will escort you from the courtroom at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, briefly, how is this relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are merely opposing what the OTP put forward about the character of the order issued by Mr. Stanisic. I believe it is -- it was dated the 15th of May. In which he deals with the same topic in the same way the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH dealt with it because it is his legal obligation to do so. And here we see that this is done at this level too. The OTP characterised this act of Mr. Stanisic in one way, and we are opposing it by claiming that this is merely a uniform application of the law, and we have shown a document to prove our point. No more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you assist us. Does the proposition have a view on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For the moment I don't have faintest idea of what document that Stanisic signed Mr. Cvijetic is talking about. So if he would like to give us the number, that would help. I don't believe when he says, We characterised it in a way, without knowing what the document is, I can't say how he characterised what. It may well be it's simply a document we put in to show the progression of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be brief. It is Exhibit 1D46 from the 65 ter list. It's an order issued by Mr. Stanisic. About the establishment of the staff ... 1D46.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
